summary: Extends BGP to carry Autonomous System numbers as four-octet values instead of the two-octet encoding in the base specification. It obsoletes RFC 4893 and updates RFC 4271. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6793 extends BGP so Autonomous System numbers can use four octets instead of two. It also defines how new and older BGP speakers exchange routes during a gradual transition.

questions: what is a four-octet as number
how do old and new bgp speakers interoperate
subtitle: How BGP carries four-octet Autonomous System numbers while supporting older speakers.

tldr.problem: The base BGP specification encodes Autonomous System numbers in two octets, and the available two-octet pool was expected to run out.
tldr.mechanism: A capability advertises four-octet support. New optional transitive attributes preserve four-octet path and aggregator information when routes pass through speakers that use only two-octet values.
tldr.outcome: Speakers can transition gradually, with defined rules for translating and reconstructing AS paths. RFC 6793 obsoletes RFC 4893 and updates RFC 4271.

today: RFC 6793 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2012. It obsoletes RFC 4893 and updates RFC 4271; the batch metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 6793.

sections.title: Why BGP Needed More AS Numbers
sections.content:
The base BGP specification, RFC 4271, encodes an Autonomous System (AS) number as a two-octet value. RFC 6793 extends BGP to carry four-octet AS numbers and expands the range from 0-65535 to 0-4294967295.

The extension is designed for a gradual change. It defines a capability for speakers to announce support, plus path attributes that can preserve four-octet information across BGP speakers that do not understand the extension. This document obsoletes RFC 4893 and updates RFC 4271.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP's original field could hold only two-octet AS numbers. This RFC adds four-octet numbers and a transition method so older speakers can still exchange routes.

sections.title: The Capability and New Attributes
sections.content:
A BGP speaker that supports four-octet numbers advertises capability code 65. The capability value contains the speaker's own AS number in four octets, and its length is four. When two new speakers support the capability, the existing AS_PATH and AGGREGATOR attributes carry four-octet numbers.

For communication through older speakers, RFC 6793 adds optional transitive attributes AS4_PATH and AS4_AGGREGATOR, which carry four-octet information. A two-octet number can be represented in four octets by setting the high-order octets to zero. A number that cannot be represented that way uses the reserved two-octet value AS_TRANS in a two-octet field.
sections.plainLanguage: New speakers announce that they understand four-octet numbers. When an older speaker is in the route, a stand-in number fits its fields while extra attributes preserve the longer values.

sections.title: When Both Speakers Support Four-Octet Numbers
sections.content:
When both BGP speakers advertise the four-octet capability to each other, each uses the AS number in the capability rather than the two-octet My Autonomous System field in the OPEN message. They encode AS numbers in sent AS_PATH and AGGREGATOR attributes using four octets and interpret received values the same way.

In this exchange, the speakers must not send AS4_PATH or AS4_AGGREGATOR. If a new speaker receives either attribute from another new speaker, it discards that attribute and continues processing the UPDATE message.
sections.plainLanguage: When both speakers support the extension, they use four-octet numbers directly in the existing path attributes. They do not need the extra transition attributes.

sections.title: Exchanging Routes with Older Speakers
sections.content:
A new speaker sends the AS_PATH to an older peer using two-octet values. It substitutes AS_TRANS for each number that cannot fit, preserving the path length. It also sends the four-octet path in AS4_PATH unless every number is mappable to two octets. An old speaker passes this optional transitive attribute along unchanged.

When a new speaker receives both attributes, it reconstructs the path using the leading part of AS_PATH and AS4_PATH. If AS_PATH has fewer AS numbers than AS4_PATH, the new attribute is ignored. Otherwise, the leading AS_PATH portion is prepended so the reconstructed path has the same number of entries as AS_PATH. Some route aggregation by old speakers can make exact reconstruction impossible.

For an aggregator whose number is not mappable, the sender puts the value in AS4_AGGREGATOR and puts AS_TRANS in AGGREGATOR.
sections.plainLanguage: A new speaker sends an older peer a short version of the path plus a longer copy in a separate attribute. When the route reaches a new speaker, it combines the two copies where the information still matches.

sections.title: Handling Malformed Attributes
sections.content:
RFC 6793 uses the attribute-discard approach for malformed AS4_PATH and AS4_AGGREGATOR attributes: the receiver discards the bad attribute, logs the event as recommended and continues processing the UPDATE. A new speaker also discards these attributes if it receives them from another new speaker.

AS4_PATH is malformed if its length is invalid, a path-segment length is zero or inconsistent, or a segment type is not defined. AS4_AGGREGATOR is malformed if its length is not 8. Confederation segment types are not allowed in AS4_PATH; a receiver discards those segments and continues.
sections.plainLanguage: If a four-octet path attribute is malformed, the speaker drops that attribute and continues processing the route update. This lets other information in the update remain usable.

sections.title: Transition Limits and Communities
sections.content:
An AS using a two-octet number may upgrade its BGP speakers one at a time. But if the AS wants to use a four-octet number as its own, all speakers in that AS must support four-octet numbers first. A non-mappable four-octet number cannot be used as a Confederation member number until all speakers in the Confederation have transitioned.

The BGP Communities attribute carries an AS number in two octets, so it cannot represent a non-mappable four-octet number. Such speakers should use four-octet AS-specific extended communities instead. Lost path information after aggregation can also create a routing-loop risk in some cases.
sections.plainLanguage: An AS can upgrade speakers gradually while keeping its existing two-octet number. It must wait for all speakers to support the extension before adopting a four-octet number for itself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the extension does not change BGP's underlying security issues, with two additional concerns. Inconsistency between AS_PATH and AS4_PATH can lose path information and create routing loops in certain cases; an attacker could exploit that result.

Using a non-mappable four-octet number as a Confederation member number before all speakers have upgraded is a misconfiguration. It weakens AS path loop detection within that Confederation.
sections.plainLanguage: If the two path attributes disagree, routers may lose information needed to detect a routing loop. A Confederation also needs every speaker upgraded before it uses a non-mappable four-octet member number.
